Here are some smart and flavorful ways to use up your baby's leftovers. ### 1.   Glaze or Marinate with Baby Food   Baby food can be a delicious alternative to store-bought glazes and marinades. Fruity options like peach, pear, or apple puree work wonderfully as sweet glazes for meats like chicken, salmon, or pork. Simply brush the puree onto the meat during the last few minutes of cooking for a naturally sweet and colorful finish. For a savory twist, try using vegetable or meat-based purees—like tomato or lentil—as a base for marinades. Mix in herbs, garlic, or spices for extra flavor. ### 2.   Hide the Baby Food in Soups   Soups are a great way to incorporate leftover baby food without anyone noticing it’s there, especially for picky eaters or when adding extra nutrients to a meal. Stir in a scoop of pureed carrots, sweet potatoes, or pumpkin into chicken soup, lentil soup, or vegetable broth. This method is excellent for reducing food waste and ensuring that the nutrients in the baby food aren’t going to waste. ### 3.   Add It as a Binder to Meat Recipes   If you're making ground meat dishes like meatballs, burgers, or meatloaf, leftover baby food can act as a natural binder—replacing things like egg or breadcrumbs. Purees like butternut squash, mashed peas, or Apple-Cinnamon baby food add moisture and flavor while helping the meat mixture stick together. Not only does this add a nutrition boost, but it can also enhance the texture of the final dish. ### 4.   Mix It with Eggs   Eggs can be a great partner to baby food in the kitchen. When making scrambled eggs, omelets, or even fried rice, blend your leftover puree into beaten eggs. For instance, a spoonful of banana puree can add natural sweetness to breakfast, while tomato or spinach puree can deliver a savory kick. Try combining the baby food with the egg whites before adding yolks to incorporate more air and fluff. ### 5.   Add It to Pasta or Rice Recipes   Pasta and rice are blank canvases for adding flavor, and baby food can be a great way to dress them up.

How to Maximize Your IRS Tax Deductions   Maximizing your tax deductions is a smart way to lower your taxable income and keep more of your hard-earned money. By leveraging both standard and itemized deductions, you can significantly reduce your tax burden. Below are several key strategies to help you get the most out of your tax return. --- ###   1. Make Charitable Contributions Appropriately   If you donate to qualified charities, you can deduct these contributions if you itemize your deductions. The IRS allows you to deduct cash, goods, or property donations, provided you keep proper records. For cash donations, be sure to obtain a written acknowledgment from the charity. For property valued over $500, you may need to file   Form 8283  . You can also carry forward unused charitable deductions for up to five years if the total exceeds your deduction limit for the current year. To make the most of this, consider bunching several years' worth of donations into one tax year if you exceed itemization limits in a given year. --- ###   2. Deduct Losses Due to Casualty, Disaster or Theft   If your property is damaged or destroyed in a federally declared disaster (such as a hurricane, wildfire, or flood), or if it is stolen, you may be eligible to claim a deduction for the loss. You can deduct the fair market value of the lost or damaged property, reduced by any insurance reimbursements or compensation you receive. Be sure to check the IRS’s list of declared disaster areas and maintain thorough documentation, including photos, appraisals, and insurance information. If filing a casualty or theft loss, you must also file   Form 4684   and report the loss on   Schedule A (Itemized Deductions)  . --- ###   3. Claim Deductions for Eligible Educator Expenses   Teachers, instructors, and certain educational staff may be eligible to deduct up to $300 ($600 if married filing jointly) for out-of-pocket classroom expenses. These can include items like school supplies, classroom technology, books, and professional development materials. The   form 1040 Schedule 1   is used to report this deduction. Even if you don’t itemize your deductions, the educator expense deduction is still available and is not subject to the 2% AGI floor (which limits many other itemized deductions on Schedule A if you itemize). Just be aware that this line is separate from the individual's own education deductions, such as college tuition. --- ###   4. Claim a Tax Credit for Child and Dependent Care   If you pay for childcare or dependent care to work or look for work, you may qualify for the   Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit  .

How to Beat Level 65 on Candy Crush   Candy Crush Saga is a game that keeps players on their toes with increasingly difficult levels and unique obstacles. Level 65 is particularly notorious for its tricky caged candies, chocolate pools, and tight scoring requirements. However, with the right strategy and a bit of patience, you can conquer it and move on to the next challenge. ###   1. Consider Restarting the Level Until You Get a Favorable Initial Position   Before you dive too deep, assess the initial candy layout. If it’s chaotic or you can't seem to make any moves that clear the board, don't be afraid to restart the level. Sometimes, even a minor difference in the candy setup can make a world of difference. On Level 65, a good initial position with enough color matches and a clear path to the chocolates is crucial. ###   2. Make the Chocolate Your First Priority   One of the main challenges of Level 65 is the large pool of chocolate covering a section of the board. Your primary objective should be to clear enough candy matches to uncover the chocolate and break it down. Aim to directly hit the chocolate with color bombs, wrapped candies, or other powerful combinations. This shortens your work as it allows you to start clearing the chocolates faster. ###   3. Concentrate on Freeing the “Caged” Candy   In this level, you often encounter candies that are trapped in cages or barriers. These candies must be set free before you can swap them. Prioritize moves that free these candies as soon as possible. Once they're out, they become part of the game and can be swapped to unleash more powerful moves or clear out obstacles like the chocolate. ###   4. Make and Use as Much Striped Candy as You Can   Striped candies are incredibly useful in Level 65. They clear an entire row or column when matched with a regular candy. Create striped candies early by making a T-shaped match (a 2x2 color match with one candy adjacent to form a “T”). Keep an eye on the board for opportunities to combine stripeds with other candies to create explosive combinations. ###   5. Use Striped Candy to Hit the Sides of the Board   Striking the sides with a horizontal or vertical striped candy can cause massive chain reactions. This technique is especially beneficial for clearing large portions of the board and uncovering hidden or blocked candies.

The Fourth of July is a time of celebration marked by fireworks, music, and festivities. However, for dogs, it can be a very stressful and dangerous event due to loud noises, unfamiliar people, and unsafe items like food and fireworks. Taking steps to ensure your dog's safety is essential. By making a few simple preparations, you can protect your furry friend and help them feel more secure. First, decide if your dog will be staying in a safe indoor space or in a secure area outside. If your dog becomes anxious or frightened by loud noises, it's best to keep them indoors in a quiet and dark room during the fireworks. Designate a pre-decided, comfortable space for your dog—such as a bedroom or a crate lined with soft bedding—to reduce stress and the urge to escape. Secure all windows and doors so your dog cannot get out unexpectedly. If your dog will be staying with you in the house, make sure he is kept far away from any food, especially if you're having guests over. Dogs can become destructive in their search for food, and human foods like chocolate, grapes, onions, and alcohol can be toxic to them. Keep countertops and tables clear, and consider feeding your dog earlier in the day if necessary. Stay calm and alert to help your dog remain calm as well. Dogs are sensitive to the emotions of their owners, so your calm demeanor can help reduce your dog's anxiety. Speak in a soothing tone, offer reassurance, and avoid showing fear of the fireworks yourself. You might also consider playing soft music or using a white noise machine to help drown out the scary sounds. Watch out for stray fireworks, which are extremely dangerous for dogs. Never buy or use fireworks, and if you're at a public event, make sure your dog is leashed and under control at all times. If your dog escapes the house or the area, contact local animal control or post a social media alert with photos and location details to ensure a quick recovery. Lastly, be prepared to have your dog’s identification current and visible. A well-fitting collar with an ID tag and updated microchip information can help reunite you with your dog if they become lost. You might also consider crate training to provide a safe retreat for your dog during stressful times.

How to Persevere   Perseverance is not just about pushing through challenges; it's about staying dedicated to your goals when things don’t go as planned. Whether you're working toward a personal milestone or pursuing a long-term ambition, perseverance keeps you going when the road gets tough. Here's how to develop and maintain the strength and mindset to persevere through any obstacle.   1. Know what you want.   Before you can persevere, you need to have a clear vision of your goals. Write them down, review them often, and understand why they matter to you. Knowing what you're working toward gives you the motivation to keep going even when progress is slow.   2. Get rid of self-doubt.   Self-doubt is a major roadblock to perseverance. Replace negative thoughts with positive affirmations, and focus on your strengths. Remember past successes and what you’ve already accomplished—this can help reinforce your confidence.   3. Practice staying cool.   Emotional reactions can derail progress. Stay calm during setbacks and avoid letting anxiety or frustration take control. Deep breathing, taking breaks, or rewriting your thoughts can help reset your mindset.   4. Don’t get dragged down by haters.   It's human nature for some people to doubt or criticize your goals. Instead of letting negativity affect you, remind yourself that their opinions don’t define your path. Focus on your values and stay grounded in what you know is right for you.   5. Know your values.   Understanding your core values helps you assess whether your goals are aligned with who you are. When you're true to your values, perseverance becomes a natural response—because you're not just working toward an external goal, but an internal sense of purpose.   6. Figure out if you’re enjoying life.   Perseverance can be challenging if you're unhappy in general. Take time to reflect on your current lifestyle and see if it’s supporting your well-being. A happy, balanced life renews your energy and ability to keep going.   7. Face reality.   Avoid denial when setbacks occur. Be honest about your situation, assess where you went wrong, and adjust as needed. Accepting the truth allows you to take action and keep moving forward with clarity.   8. Weigh your options carefully.   When faced with a tough decision, take the time to map out your options and their potential outcomes. This helps you approach challenges in a logical, strategic way rather than reacting impulsively.

How to Support the Natural Resources Defense Council   Supporting the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) is a powerful way to contribute to environmental and public health advocacy on local, national, and global levels. Founded in 1970, the NRDC is one of the largest and most influential environmental advocacy organizations in the United States. Whether you're looking to make a one-time donation, plan a long-term legacy of support, or help the organization through financial gifts, there are several effective ways to give.   Meet with an Estate Planning Attorney   If you're considering making a lasting impact, one of the best steps is to meet with an estate planning attorney. They can help you make informed decisions about how to include the NRDC in your will or trusts. During the consultation, your attorney can outline various legal structures for gifting—such as bequests, charitable remainder trusts, or charitable lead trusts—and help you understand how these strategies can align with your personal financial goals while benefiting the NRDC.   Consider Leaving Assets to the NRDC   Many people choose to support the NRDC through a bequest in their will or revocable living trust. By designating the NRDC as a beneficiary of a portion of your assets—such as property, securities, retirement accounts, or life insurance—you can leave a lasting legacy. Leaving assets to the NRDC ensures your support continues to make a difference long after you're gone, and it often provides important tax benefits for the estate.   Make a Gift That Will Pay You Income   A charitable remainder trust is a financial tool that allows you to receive income during your lifetime while also supporting the NRDC. When you fund a trust with cash or appreciated assets, the trust distributes income to you or a beneficiary for a set number of years or for life. After your income period ends, the remaining assets in the trust are transferred to the NRDC. Not only can this provide a steady stream of income, but it also allows you to potentially deduct the future value of your gift for income tax purposes.   Consider a Charitable Lead Trust   If you have significant assets and would like to support the NRDC while also benefiting loved ones, a charitable lead trust could be an ideal option. With this type of trust, the NRDC receives income for a specific period (usually 10–20 years), after which the remaining assets are transferred to the trust's named beneficiaries—typically family members.

How to Showcase Your Skills   Effectively showcasing your skills is essential when competing for job opportunities, promotions, or even when building a strong professional reputation. Whether you're in an interview, networking event, or collaborating on a project, demonstrating your abilities confidently and concretely can make a powerful impression. Below are practical steps to help you showcase your skills in a compelling and authentic way. ---   1. Speak Confidently About Your Skills and Abilities   Confidence is key when discussing your strengths. Avoid understating your capabilities or expressing self-doubt. Instead, use assertive language and be clear about what you can do. For example, instead of saying, “I  think  I’m good with project management,” say, “I successfully managed a team of five on a tight deadline, delivering the project two weeks ahead of schedule.” Tone and body language also play a role: maintain eye contact, sit or stand with good posture, and speak with clarity. When you present your skills this way, you project authority and competence. ---   2. Provide Examples to Prove Your Skills   Merely stating that you have a skill isn’t enough—you need to back it up with evidence. Use the   STAR method   (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to frame your stories clearly. For example: -   Situation:   “I was assigned to improve customer satisfaction for a product launch with a tight budget.” -   Task:   “My task was to develop and implement a cost-effective marketing strategy.” -   Action:   “I conducted customer surveys, analyzed feedback, and proposed an influencer partnership.” -   Result:   “The campaign exceeded targets by 20%, and customer feedback scores increased by 15%.” Specific examples like this demonstrate initiative, problem-solving, and results—key traits any employer values. ---   3. Have a Portfolio Available to View in an Interview   A portfolio showcases your work and provides a visual representation of your skills. This is particularly effective for creative roles (graphic design, writing, programming), but can also work for analysts, engineers, or project managers. Your portfolio should include: - Strong samples of your best work. - Descriptions of your role in each project. - The skills you used and the impact you made. - Any client or user feedback (if appropriate). A digital version can be hosted on a personal website or platforms like LinkedIn, Behance, or GitHub. In an interview, ask if the interviewer would like to review it. Having a portfolio can set you apart from candidates who rely only on verbal descriptions. ---   4. Demonstrate Your Relevant Soft Skills During Meetings   Soft skills like communication, leadership, and teamwork are equally important as hard skills and can’t be assessed from a résumé alone.

How to Develop Relative Pitch1   Relative pitch is the ability to identify or reproduce a given musical note by comparing it to a reference note. Whether you're a musician looking to enhance your ear training or a hobbyist aiming to better understand music, developing relative pitch can elevate your skills and deepen your connection to sound. Here’s how to start on your journey. ---   1. Know How Intervals Are Named   Intervals are the building blocks of relative pitch. Understanding how they are named helps you recognize their unique sound. An interval is the distance between two musical notes and is measured in "half steps" or "semitones." Common intervals include: -   Unison (0 half steps):   Same note. -   Minor second (1 half step):   Dissonant, tense (e.g., "C" to "C#"). -   Major second (2 half steps):   A step apart (e.g., "C" to "D"). -   Minor third (3 half steps):   Hints of sadness. -   Major third (4 half steps):   Bright and happy. -   Fourth (5 half steps):   Open and stable, often described as "angelic" (e.g., "C" to "F"). -   Fifth (7 half steps):   Strong, powerful – rhythm of Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy.” -   Octave (12 half steps):   Same note but higher. Learning the names and characteristics of intervals will help you describe what you hear and associate each with a distinct emotional or tonal quality. ---   2. Use Reference Songs   Assign familiar songs to different intervals or chord progressions as a reference tool. For example: -   Major third:   The first two notes in “Kiss the Girl” ("Somewhere in the world..."). -   Perfect fourth:   “Here Comes the Bride” starts with a perfect fourth. -   Perfect fifth:   The first two notes of “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” These associations act as anchors for your ear. When you hear a similar interval in a different song, you can instantly recognize it using your memory. ---   3. Practice Solfege   Solfege is a system of assigning syllables (do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, do) to pitches. It's a powerful method for developing relative pitch because it allows you to internalize the relationships between notes. Try the following: - Sing a simple scale, labeling each note with its solfege syllable. - Identify the scale degree of any played note after hearing the tonic (starting note). - Use a tuning fork or app to establish a reference tone and practice naming notes using solfege. Consistent practice with solfege trains your brain to “hear” the structure of melodies. ---   4. Try the Nike Method   Inspired by Nike’s slogan—"Just do it!"—this approach involves small, consistent practice.

To start a foundation, you must first apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). The EIN is essential for tax purposes and is required to open a bank account, file taxes, and manage payroll for your foundation. You can apply for an EIN online through the IRS website, by mail, or by fax. The process is free, and you’ll need to provide basic information about your foundation, such as its name, address, and the name and title of an authorized individual. The EIN is typically issued immediately if you apply online, so plan to complete this step early in the foundation-establishment process. Once you have your EIN, the next step is to fill out IRS Form 1023, which is the Application for Recognition of Exemption. This is the primary application required by the IRS if you are forming a public charity and want to be recognized as a tax-exempt organization under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code. Form 1023 asks for detailed information about your foundation, including its purpose, governance structure, financial projections, and how it will fund its activities. You must include a copy of your organization’s articles of incorporation and bylaws with the form. For smaller foundations, there is also a shorter version called Form 1023-EZ that may be used if your projected gross receipts are under $50,000 per year and your expenses don’t exceed certain thresholds. Filing Form 1023 can be a lengthy and complex process, so it may be wise to consult with a tax professional or attorney to ensure that you fulfill all requirements and submit the form correctly. After your foundation has been granted tax-exemption status, you must continue to file annual tax returns with the IRS. For private foundations, the required form is IRS Form 990-PF. This form is used to report the foundation’s income, expenses, investments, and charitable contributions, as well as the compensation of officers, directors, and key employees. Failure to file Form 990-PF on time can result in penalties, so it’s important to keep accurate financial records and submit the form annually as of the end of your fiscal year. The IRS provides detailed instructions with the form, so it's important to carefully follow these to ensure compliance. If your foundation is organized as a trust rather than a corporation or LLC, you may also need to file IRS Form 5227 along with Form 990-PF.

How to Tell Someone You Are Bisexual   Coming out as bisexual can be an empowering and emotional experience. Taking the step to share who you truly are with someone is a powerful act of self-acceptance and courage. Before you take this step, it’s important to feel confident and ready—knowing that your sexual orientation is valid and a beautiful part of who you are. Here are some thoughtful steps to guide you through the process of telling someone you are bisexual.   Be confident in who you are!   Before you tell anyone else, take time to understand and accept your own identity. Being bisexual means being attracted to people of more than one gender, and recognizing this truth about yourself is the first—and most important—step. When you feel secure in your own skin, you’ll be able to share your identity with others in a more assured, positive way.   Consider who you want to tell first.   You don’t have to tell everyone at once. Think about who is emotionally supportive and trustworthy in your life—perhaps a close friend, a sibling, or a partner. Choose someone who you believe will listen with an open heart and mind. It's important to feel comfortable and safe in the environment you choose to share with.   Carefully consider telling your parent(s) at this time.   This can be a big decision and will vary depending on your relationship with your parents. If you’re concerned, consider talking to someone first to support you or guide you through the process. It’s okay to wait until the time feels right for you.   Consider that many people do not have a clear understanding of what it means to be bisexual.   You may encounter questions or misconceptions—such as the belief that being bisexual means you’re indecisive or that you are "just going through a phase." Be prepared to explain what being bisexual means to you, but remember that it’s not your responsibility to educate everyone. Not everyone will understand at first, and that’s okay.   Be calm and rational; be sure of what you are saying and explain that this is simply who you are.   Come out as bisexual in a way that feels true to your story. You can share how you feel and why being open about your identity is important to your happiness and well-being. Let the person know that you want to be seen for who you truly are.

How to Help Kids Find a Sport They Enjoy2   Finding a sport or physical activity that a child truly enjoys can be a rewarding yet challenging process. Every child is unique, with different interests, energy levels, and preferences. The goal is to help your child discover an activity they enjoy, which will encourage them to stay active, build confidence, and develop new skills. Here are some strategies to help guide them. ### Consider Other Fitness Opportunities for Kids Sports aren’t the only way to get moving and stay healthy. Fitness opportunities such as gymnastics, dance, martial arts, or yoga can also be excellent options for kids, especially those who may not feel drawn to team sports. These activities often allow for personal expression, offer mental and physical discipline, and can be more flexible in terms of participation. Try scouting local classes or community centers that offer these programs to give your child a broader range of experiences. ### Mention Athletic Options for Kids Who Like Music If your child is musical, consider integrating that passion with physical activity. Drumming or dance-based workouts are perfect for kids who love rhythm, beat, or movement. There are also sports like rhythmic gymnastics or even marching band, which involve both music and physical coordination. By tapping into your child’s current interests, you’re more likely to keep them engaged in something they enjoy. ### Try Outdoor Sports with Your Kid Sometimes, kids who are hesitant about structured sports enjoy the freedom and variety of outdoor activities. Consider trying sports like hiking, biking, frisbee, or even capture the flag in a park setting. These activities are less formal, allow for creativity, and can be adapted to your child’s energy level. Engaging in outdoor play together as a family can also help your child feel more comfortable experimenting with new types of movement and develop a love for being outdoors. ### Ask Your Kid if They’d Be More Interested in Physical Activity That Includes Animals Some kids are naturally drawn to animals and enjoy physical activity that involves them. Activities such as horseback riding, dog agility courses, or even herding activities (such as with sheep or goats on a farm) can be great ways to encourage fitness while combining it with a passion for animals. If your child mentions an interest in animals, consider exploring local stables, pet therapy programs, or pet-related adventures to keep them physically active in a fun, engaging way.

To start the installation of a domain controller, you need to add the Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) role. To do this, click on the   Server Manager   tile from the Start screen, select   Manage  , and then choose   Add Roles and Features  . In the Add Roles and Features wizard, click   Next   past the   Before You Begin   screen. Choose   Role-based or feature-based installation   and click   Next  . Choose the destination server by selecting   Select a server from the server pool  , making sure the   localhost   or the target server is selected, then click   Next  . Under the   Server Roles   section, scroll to   Active Directory Domain Services  , and click   Add Features   when prompted. This will automatically add the required features. Once all dependencies are met, click   Next  . After reviewing the selections, click   Next   again, and then   Install   to proceed with the role installation. The installation will take a few minutes to complete. Once the installation is complete, in the Server Manager, you’ll see a yellow dialog box stating that   Active Directory Domain Services has been added successfully  —click   Promote this server to a domain controller  . In the next step, you’ll be prompted to   Add a New Forest  . Make sure to enter the correct domain name in the   Root domain name for the new forest   field (e.g., `example.com`). You can also configure the   Domain Functional Level   and   Forest Functional Level   if needed. How to Make a Beekeeping Suit   If you're preparing to start beekeeping or want a personalized beekeeping suit that fits like a glove and offers maximum protection, making one at home is a great option. This DIY suit ensures a close fit, full coverage, and built-in convenience like Velcro fastenings and a hat attachment. Follow these clear steps to build your own custom suit.   Step 1: Choose a White Button-Down Shirt   Start by selecting a white, long-sleeved button-down shirt. It should be easy to move in and preferably made from a thick, durable material like cotton or a cotton-polyester blend. The color is important because bees are less likely to be agitated by light-colored garments.   Step 2: Gather Other Supplies   You’ll need the following materials: - A white button-down shirt - Durable, light-colored fabric for the veil - A wide-brimmed hat (preferably white or light color) - A sewing kit - Scissors - Measuring tape - Velcro (both hook and loop) - Elastic fabric for neck and wrists - Extra strong thread for durability   Step 3: Remove the Buttons from the Shirt   You won’t need the buttons for fastening, so go ahead and remove them. This will make it easier to modify the shirt later.   Step 4: Sew the Button Holes Closed   To create a smooth, tight front seam, sew over the button holes to close them. This will help maintain the integrity of the Velcro you’ll be adding in the next step.   Step 5: Cut Velcro to Line the Shirt Opening   Measure the front opening of the shirt and cut strips of Velcro (hook and loop) that match in length. Step 7: Cut and Attach Velcro Around the Collar and Sleeves   Add additional strips of Velcro around the collar and at the bottom of the sleeves. This helps keep the suit sealed at the neck and wrists, preventing bees from getting in.   Step 8: Choose a Wide-Brimmed Hat   A wide-brimmed hat with a ribbon around the brim is ideal for attaching the veil to later.

How to Diagnose Hypothyroidism in Golden Retrievers   Golden Retrievers are prone to hereditary conditions like hypothyroidism, a condition in which the thyroid gland under-produces essential hormones that regulate metabolism. This hormonal imbalance affects nearly all body systems and can lead to a range of symptoms if not addressed. Knowing how to recognize and diagnose hypothyroidism early is important for your dog's overall health and well-being.   Be aware of how hypothyroidism develops in your golden retriever.   Hypothyroidism typically develops in middle-aged dogs, around the age of 4 to 6 years. It often results from autoimmune thyroiditis, a condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the thyroid gland, gradually destroying its ability to function properly. Myxedema, a related condition involving hormone deficiency and skin thickening, is also common in affected dogs. Since this is a breed-specific susceptibility, Golden Retrievers require watchful attention during this stage of life.   Note if your dog has low energy.   One of the most noticeable symptoms of hypothyroidism is a dramatic drop in energy levels. Your dog may become lethargic and show little interest in activities they once enjoyed, such as walking, playing fetch, or going for swims. This lack of motivation is often mistaken for aging, but if it occurs without a clear reason like illness or injury, it should raise a red flag.   Check if your dog starts to gain weight.   Thyroid hormones are vital for regulating metabolism. If the thyroid is underactive, your dog may gain weight even if their activity level and food intake remain the same. This weight gain is typically uncontrollable through diet or exercise and is often paired with a lack of energy and abnormal heat retention.   Look at your dog’s coat for any dullness or patchiness.   The thyroid plays a key role in maintaining healthy skin and a glossy coat. Hypothyroid dogs often develop dry, brittle fur, a dull coat, or hair loss, especially on the tail, sides, and back. The skin may become oily or inflamed, and you might notice symmetrical hair thinning, which is a strong indicator of a thyroid problem.   Check your dog’s heart rate.   A slower than normal heart rate (bradycardia) is another sign of hypothyroidism. This can be noticed during the physical exam or go unnoticed unless the veterinarian checks it. Along with a weak pulse, cold intolerance (your dog shivering without a reason in mild temperatures), and high cholesterol due to slower fat processing are also potential symptoms.

How to File for Bankruptcy Without an Attorney   Filing for bankruptcy can seem like a daunting and complex process, especially when you factor in the costs of hiring legal representation. However, it is entirely possible to file for bankruptcy on your own, as long as you are organized, informed, and dedicated to following the process carefully. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you file for bankruptcy   without an attorney  .   Find an Approved Agency   Before you file, you must complete credit counseling and financial management courses. The U.S. Trustee Program maintains a list of approved agencies that offer these services. Choose a local or online provider that is certified under the Bankruptcy Code. This is a mandatory requirement regardless of whether you hire an attorney or do it yourself.   Gather Financial Documents   You’ll need to provide detailed financial information about your income, debts, assets, and expenses. Gather the following: -   Identification:   Government-issued ID, Social Security number, driver’s license. -   Tax returns:   For the past two years. -   Account statements:   Recent bank, credit card, and investment statements. -   Proof of income:   Pay stubs or employer letters showing your monthly salary or income sources. -   Debt lists:   A comprehensive list of all creditors, what you owe, and contact information. -   Schedules of assets and liabilities:   Detail what you own and what you owe.   Get Copies of Your Credit Reports   Order free copies of your credit reports from the three major credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Review these for errors, and use them to compile an accurate list of your debts and creditors.   Meet with Your Counselor   Once you’ve gathered your documents and credit reports, schedule a meeting with your certified credit counselor. They will review your financial situation and help you determine the best type of bankruptcy for your needs—Chapter 7 or Chapter 13.   Evaluate the Counselor's Budget and Plan   Your counselor will provide you with a budget and a debt repayment plan. Even if you choose to file for bankruptcy, it is a good idea to explore alternatives, such as debt management or consolidation. If your counselor confirms that bankruptcy is your best option, they will also help you with your plan moving forward.   Get a Certificate of Completion   After your counseling sessions, the agency will issue a   certificate of credit counseling  . This is required to be submitted with your bankruptcy petition. You’ll also receive a separate   certificate of completion   for the financial management course.

How to Detect Ovarian Cancer   Ovarian cancer can be difficult to detect in its early stages because it often presents with subtle or vague symptoms. However, catching the disease early is critical for successful treatment. If you are experiencing any unusual symptoms or have a family history of ovarian or breast cancer, take the following steps to seek early detection and medical care.   Identify Possible Symptoms   Be aware of the signs and symptoms that may indicate ovarian cancer. Common symptoms include abdominal bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, difficulty eating or feeling full quickly, frequent urination, and persistent fatigue. Other signs may include gas, nausea, or changes in bowel habits like constipation. If these symptoms last for more than two weeks and are new to you, consult your doctor.   Consider Whether You May Have a Higher Risk   Certain factors increase the risk of ovarian cancer. These include a family history of ovarian or breast cancer (especially if someone in your family tested positive for BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene mutations), age (risk increases after menopause), obesity, and never having been pregnant. If you have multiple risk factors, speak with your doctor about regular screenings or genetic counseling.   Learn About the Different Types of Ovarian Cancers   Ovarian cancer is not one disease but a group of illnesses. The most common is   epithelial ovarian cancer  , which develops in the outer layer of the ovaries. Less common types include   germ cell tumors   (which form in the egg-producing cells) and   stromal tumors   (which grow from the connective tissue in the ovaries). Understanding the type can help your doctor determine the best diagnostic and treatment approach.   Get a Pelvic Exam   Your doctor will likely begin with a   pelvic exam   to check for signs of tumors or swelling in the ovaries. During the exam, the doctor will use a gloved hand to feel for abnormalities in the pelvic area and may perform a   transvaginal ultrasound   for a better look at the ovaries.   Discuss Imaging Tests with Your Doctor   Imaging tests can help provide a clearer picture of the ovaries. A   transvaginal ultrasound   is often used to examine the size, shape, and texture of the ovaries. A   CT scan   or   MRI   may be used to see if the cancer has spread to other organs. These tests can help your doctor determine the extent of the disease.   Consider a Blood Test   One of the most common blood tests used to detect ovarian cancer is the   CA-125 test  .

How to Avoid Being Oversensitive   Being oversensitive can make simple interactions feel overwhelming. While emotional sensitivity can also be a strength—allowing for deep empathy and creativity—unhealthy levels of sensitivity can lead to unnecessary stress, misunderstandings, and strained relationships. Learning how to manage and reduce being oversensitive is not about becoming emotionally detached but rather building emotional resilience and perspective. Here are some effective strategies to help you avoid being oversensitive.   1. Reflect on Your Emotions   Before reacting to a situation, take a moment to understand what’s triggering your sensitivity. Ask yourself questions like: Is this issue really about me or the other person? Am I reading too much into this? Reflecting can help you differentiate between the real issue and your interpretation of it.   2. Analyze Your Role in the Issues   Sometimes, oversensitivity stems from taking things personally or assuming too much responsibility. Try to look at the situation objectively and consider whether the problem is a result of your own behavior or expectations. This can help you grow in humility and accountability, reducing the need to feel hurt or defensive.   3. Overcome This for Yourself   Shift your focus from what you're being sensitive about to what you can do instead. Redirect your energy to constructive actions like journaling, reading, or engaging in something you enjoy. This helps break the cycle of emotional reactivity.   4. Take a Deep Breath   When you feel triggered, pause and take a deep breath. Inhale slowly for four counts, hold for four counts, and exhale for four counts. This simple act can help calm your nervous system and give you space to react thoughtfully rather than impulsively.   5. Stay in the Present   Oversensitivity often involves ruminating over past events or fearing future consequences. Practice mindfulness to anchor yourself in the present. Focus on what is happening now rather than dwelling on what could have gone another way.   6. Express Yourself   Instead of bottling up your emotions, find healthy ways to express them. Talk to a trusted friend, write in a journal, or engage in any activity that lets you channel intense feelings productively. Expression reduces the pressure that builds from being oversensitive.   7. Hang in There   Changing your sensitivity requires patience and consistency. Some days will be harder than others, and setbacks are normal. Try not to get discouraged—keep practicing emotional regulation day by day.   8. Distance Yourself, Literally   If a particular situation or person repeatedly triggers your sensitivity, give yourself physical space.

How to Distinguish Employees from Non-Employees   When running a business, it's essential to know whether a person is an employee or a non-employee—such as an independent contractor, intern, or volunteer. Classifying someone incorrectly can lead to serious legal and financial consequences, as employees are entitled to certain rights and protections under labor laws. Follow these steps to determine whether an individual qualifies as an employee or not.   1. Check if the internship is related to a university.   If the internship is part of a formal academic program or structured as a credit-bearing activity coordinated by a university or college, it's more likely to be classified as a non-employee position. In these cases, the learning experience and educational objectives are typically the primary focus of the arrangement, rather than the benefit of the business.   2. Confirm that the internship is for the intern’s benefit.   An intern should gain skills, experience, and training that can be applied in a future job. If the primary beneficiary of the internship is the company and the intern isn’t receiving meaningful educational or development opportunities, it's a sign the intern may actually be an employee.   3. Check that the intern hasn’t replaced an employee.   If your intern is performing tasks and duties that a regular employee would typically do and is replacing an existing employee, this raises red flags. Employers are not allowed to use interns to sidestep labor costs or obligations to their employees. This is a key factor that U.S. labor laws consider when determining employer liability.   4. Identify why you are training the intern.   Training is a major indicator of a potential employee relationship. If the intern requires you to provide training similar to what you would give a regular employee, and the training is in place for the intern’s benefit rather than your convenience, the internship is likely not the correct classification.   5. Calculate how long the internship is.   The duration of the internship is a key consideration. Short-term, temporary internships (usually lasting no more than a few months) are more likely to qualify as non-employee internships. If the internship is extensive or ongoing, especially when it fills a role the company would otherwise hire for, it becomes more likely to be reclassified as a job.   6. Check your agreement about wages.   Do you pay the intern or provide the intern with compensation in the form of snacks, benefits, or job references?

How to Give Someone a Filling   If you suspect someone has a toothache or a cavity, it's essential to know how to address the issue temporarily until they can visit a dentist. This process can relieve pain and prevent further complications. Here's a step-by-step guide on how to give someone a filling. --- 1.   Take Pain Relievers to Address the Pain   Before attempting to manage the cavity, ensure the person takes an over-the-counter pain reliever like ibuprofen or acetaminophen. These can help reduce discomfort and inflammation caused by the decay. Be sure to follow the dosage instructions or consult with a pharmacist if uncertain. --- 2.   Apply Dental Wax to Sharp Edges   If the tooth has a sharp edge that is irritating the mouth, gently apply dental wax (available in pharmacies) over the area. The wax acts as a cushion and can make the area more comfortable until professional treatment is possible. --- 3.   Place Temporary Dental Fillings   Over-the-counter temporary dental fillings are available at most pharmacies. These fillings are not meant to last long but can help protect the tooth from further damage and reduce sensitivity. Follow the package instructions carefully when applying it. --- 4.   Consult with Your Dentist   While temporary fixes can provide relief, it's essential to book a professional appointment as soon as possible. A dentist can properly clean, treat, and fill the cavity to prevent infections or more severe issues like tooth extraction. --- 5.   Locate the Area of Decay   If the person is experiencing someone else with the cavity (e.g., a child or family member), examine the tooth carefully with a flashlight and mouth mirror. Look for dark spots, cracks, or areas where the enamel is worn or soft. This will help identify where the filling is needed. --- 6.   Numb the Tooth   Use a numbing gel that contains benzocaine and apply it to the tooth and surrounding gum area. This will help manage pain during the process. Give it about 5-10 minutes to take effect. --- 7.   Cover the Rest of the Area   Use cotton rolls or gauze to isolate the affected tooth. This helps keep the mouth dry and prevents the filling material from being washed away. You can also use a rubber dam if it's available. --- 8.   Drill Away Previous Reconstruction   If there was a previous filling, denture, or crown, it may need to be removed before placing the new one.

How to Stop Being Defensive   Being defensive is a natural response when we feel attacked or criticized. It can help us protect our ego and emotions, but it often leads to misunderstandings, arguments, and strained relationships. Learning how to stop being defensive is crucial for effective communication and personal growth. By becoming more self-aware and practicing emotional control, you can respond to situations more thoughtfully rather than react automatically. Here are some steps to help you on your journey. ###   1. Recognize the Physical Signs of Defensiveness   Defensiveness doesn’t just affect your thoughts and words—it also shows up in your body. You might notice your heart rate increase, your shoulders tense up, or your jaw clench. You may also feel heat rising to your face or a strong urge to speak before you’ve processed what someone’s saying. Being aware of these physical signals is the first step in breaking the cycle. When you notice them, pause for a moment and consciously slow down. Acknowledge that your instinct to react is kicking in and give yourself a chance to respond differently. ###   2. Take Deep Breaths   When you feel yourself getting defensive, try to take a few deep breaths. Inhale slowly through your nose, hold it for a few seconds, and then exhale through your mouth. This helps calm your nervous system and gives you time to think before you speak. Breathing deeply can help you stay grounded and prevent you from saying something you might later regret. It also shows the other person that you're making an effort to stay composed, which can help de-escalate the situation. ###   3. Don’t Interrupt   Interrupting someone when you’re feeling defensive is a common reaction, but it doesn’t help the conversation move forward in a productive way. Instead of jumping in with a rebuttal, try to listen to the full point they’re making. This not only helps you understand where they’re coming from but also allows you to formulate a calmer response. Let them finish speaking before you respond, and even then, consider whether you truly need to say something. Sometimes silence is the best response. ###   4. Ask to Have the Conversation Later   If you feel as though the conversation isn’t going constructively or if your defensiveness is getting the better of you, it’s okay to ask for a break. You might say, “Let’s go over this later when we’re both more calm,” or “I need a moment to gather my thoughts.”

How to File a Motion in Colorado   Filing a motion in Colorado is an essential part of participating in the state’s legal process, whether you are a plaintiff or defendant in a civil or criminal case. A motion is a formal request to the court to take a specific action, and following the proper procedures is crucial to ensure it’s accepted and reviewed. Below is a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process.   1. Determine the Type of Motion You Want to File   Start by identifying the type of motion you need to file. Common types include motions to dismiss, motions for summary judgment, motions to compel discovery, or motions to set a hearing. Each motion serves a unique purpose and must be tailored accordingly to your legal situation.   2. Review the Rules of Civil Procedure   Colorado has its own set of specific rules relating to the filing of motions, known as the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure (CRCP). These rules outline the requirements for how and when you can file a motion, the notice you must give to other parties, and the format of the motion itself. Make sure you are familiar with the rule that applies directly to your motion.   3. Research the Law That Supports Your Motion   Before drafting your motion, gather and review any applicable legal statutes, case law, or precedents that support your request. This will help strengthen your motion and show the court that your request is legally sound and justified.   4. Contact the Other Side   It is often good practice to communicate with the opposing party or their attorney before filing the motion. This is not always required, but it may help you understand their perspective or potentially resolve the issue without a formal motion.   5. Search for Forms   The Colorado Judicial Branch provides a variety of legal forms and resources for self-represented individuals (pro se litigants). You can find helpful documents and forms online at [Legal Forms for Colorado](https://www.courts.state.co.us/LegalForms.html). These forms may serve as templates to help you draft your motion.   6. Complete Your Documents   Draft your motion using clear, concise language. You will need to include your contact information, the case number, a title that explains the motion, and the grounds for your request. In addition, your filing must include a certificate of service (proving you informed the opposition of the motion) and any attachments or supporting documents.

Go Down a Hill (Literally)   Find a safe, small hill and have fun by racing downhill on your bike, skateboard, or just by rolling a wheeled toy like a scooter. People Watch and Immerse Yourself in the World Around You   Sometimes the best entertainment is right outside your door. How to Treat Anxiety Disorders in Elderly People   Anxiety disorders can affect anyone, regardless of age, and they are particularly common among the elderly. Anxiety often manifests differently in older adults than in younger people, making it important to recognize and address it properly. Treating anxiety in elderly individuals requires a thoughtful, patient-centered approach that coordinates physical and mental health care.   Be able to identify anxiety in the elderly.   Anxiety in seniors can often be mistaken for other conditions such as depression, dementia, or even heart problems due to overlapping symptoms. Look for behavioral signs such as restlessness, irritability, difficulty sleeping, or excessive worry. Physical symptoms can include fatigue, chest pain, rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, or gastrointestinal issues. If you or someone you care for is experiencing symptoms that interfere with daily life or cause distress, it may be time to seek help.   Start with the primary care physician.   The first step in treating anxiety is to visit a primary care doctor. Many physical ailments can mimic anxiety symptoms in older adults, such as thyroid problems, heart conditions, or vitamin deficiencies. A thorough check-up will help rule out these possibilities and confirm whether the symptoms are indeed related to anxiety. Your doctor may also ask about family medical history and grief or life changes that could be contributing factors.   Obtain a mental health referral.   Once physical causes are ruled out, your primary care physician may refer you to a mental health professional, such as a psychiatrist or psychologist, who specializes in older adults. A mental health evaluation can help identify the specific type of anxiety disorder someone may have—such as generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, or social anxiety—and determine the most appropriate treatment plan.   Recognize how medications affect aging bodies.   Medications can be part of a treatment plan for seniors with anxiety, but they must be used cautiously. Some common medications, like benzodiazepines (used for short-term anxiety relief), can have serious side effects in older adults, including drowsiness, confusion, and an increased risk of falls. A psychiatrist will consider a senior’s overall health, memory, and current medications before prescribing anything. In some cases, non-steroidal anti-anxiety medications like buspirone may be safer and more effective for long-term use.   Consider therapy.   Therapy, particularly cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), is a highly effective treatment for anxiety disorders and can work well for elderly individuals. CBT helps people understand and change the thought patterns that lead to anxiety.

How to Deal With Getting Corporal Punishment   Corporal punishment, also known as physical punishment, is any action that inflicts physical pain on a child or adult as a form of discipline. While it was once widely practiced in schools and homes, it is now a topic of debate due to ethical, legal, and psychological concerns. If you or someone you know has experienced corporal punishment, it's important to understand your legal rights, the effects of such punishment, and how to best respond. ### 1.   Check Your State's Laws   Laws regarding corporal punishment vary significantly by state and by the setting in which it occurs (e.g., school versus home). In the United States, some states still permit corporal punishment in schools, though this is becoming less common. On the other hand, most states have specific laws protecting children from physical abuse in the home, and parents who engage in violent corporal punishment may face criminal charges. You should familiarize yourself with your local laws and whether corporal punishment is legally permitted or criminalized. If the punishment occurred in a school or daycare setting and was legal under current law, your options may be limited, but if it was inappropriate or illegal, you may have grounds for a complaint or legal action. ### 2.   Understand Corporal Punishment's Limits   Even where corporal punishment is legally permitted, there are strict limits on how it can be applied. It is typically restricted to non-deadly force and must not result in injury. For example, in schools, paddling might be allowed only if it is carried out in a specific environment with supervision. If the punishment goes beyond what is allowed by school or state policy—such as excessive force or targeting a sensitive area—it is considered abuse. Understanding these boundaries is essential in determining whether the punishment crossed the line from "discipline" into "abuse." ### 3.   Look for Common Actions   Signs of physical punishment can include unexplained bruises, redness, or marks on the body. If you or someone you know is experiencing repeated pain or fear from a school or caregiver, this is a red flag. Documenting these events can be helpful if you decide to report the issue. Look for patterns, such as punishment occurring regularly, or the individual showing signs of psychological distress afterward, like anxiety or depression. ### 4.   Think About the Effects on Children   Research on the effects of corporal punishment consistently shows that it can have harmful effects on children, especially when used repeatedly.

How to End All Ties With Your Family   Ending all ties with your family is a deeply difficult and life-altering decision. It often comes out of necessity—due to emotional abuse, toxicity, addiction, or negativity—but it's essential to approach this with care and self-respect. Here's a structured guide to help you navigate this process.   Give yourself permission to set limits.   Before taking any action, recognize that setting boundaries is not selfish; it is self-preservation. If your family has hurt you or consistently respects your well-being as little as possible, you are allowed—and sometimes obligated—to protect your own mental and emotional health. Remind yourself that your right to boundaries is valid and justified regardless of their feelings or reactions.   Establish what kind of contact will be acceptable to you, if any.   Decide clearly what, if any, interactions you are willing to maintain: no contact, email-only, phone calls, or a specific time limit for visits, for example. It may mean creating "zero contact" if contact invites harm. Be as specific as possible, even if it's hard to predict. Write down your boundaries so you can refer back to them when emotions run high.   Hold up your end of the agreement.   Consistency is key when enforcing boundaries. If you commit to no communication, don’t budge just because they call or knock on your door with an emotional plea. Let your actions confirm your boundaries are final and non-negotiable. This might be painful for them—and it might shake you at times—but it’s necessary for your own safety and peace of mind.   Be prepared for intrusions.   It's common for family members to push against your limits, sometimes in frustrating or manipulative ways. They may guilt-trip you, lie about needing help, or even bad-mouth you to others. Protect yourself by setting clear consequences if they violate your boundaries (e.g., you will block their number, unblock them on social media, or avoid future requests for engagement). Stick to your word.   Seek counseling.   Ending all ties is a major step, and it can feel lonely or isolating. A professional therapist who specializes in family dynamics and estrangement can help you process your emotions, gain confidence in your decision, and build resilience. Therapy also helps you avoid decision fatigue and ensures you're emotionally supported during this transition.   Be cautious in accepting offers of help.

Draft Your Business Plan   A solid business plan is essential for the success of your money lending business. Your plan should outline your business structure, target market, loan products, interest rates, repayment terms, and financial projections. Draft Underwriting Criteria   Establish clear criteria for assessing loan applications.
